title: Engineering teams, Q3 update
paragraphs: Priya Raman leads the Firmware team. The Firmware team owns the Telemetry Gateway, the cloud service that receives data from our devices.
Tomas Berg leads the Hardware team. The Hardware team owns the Atlas-3 design and the Borealis controller design.
Ines Okafor leads Customer Support. Support escalates any defect it cannot reproduce to the team that owns the affected system, and aims to answer within one business day.

title: Atlas-3 sensor: product brief
paragraphs: The Atlas-3 is a battery-powered water-quality sensor. It sends readings every 15 minutes through the Telemetry Gateway.
The Atlas-3 main board uses the QX-7 radio chip for its cellular link. Battery life is rated at five years at the default reading interval.
The Atlas-3 housing is the IP68 enclosure, which is rated for continuous immersion to two metres.

title: Supplier register (excerpt)
paragraphs: Varnell Semi is the sole supplier of the QX-7 radio chip. The supply contract renews every January.
Tessaly Plastics supplies the IP68 enclosure. We own the tooling for the enclosure, so a second moulder could be qualified within a quarter.

title: Borealis controller: release notes 2.4
paragraphs: Borealis 2.4 adds Modbus support. The Borealis controller now takes power from the PM-2 power module, which replaces the older PM-1.
The PM-2 power module is made by Varnell. Firmware updates for the controller are delivered through the Telemetry Gateway.
The controller design is maintained by T. Berg and the Hardware team.

title: Key accounts
paragraphs: Osterby Water Utility runs 420 Atlas-3 units across its reservoirs and treatment plants. It renewed its service plan in May.
Calder Grain Co-op monitors silo humidity with 60 Atlas 3 units.
Pellham Labs uses the Borealis controller to run its environmental test chambers.

title: Incident review: QX-7 shipment delay
paragraphs: On 3 March 2026, Varnell Semiconductor told us that QX-7 shipments would slip by six weeks because of a wafer shortage.
The review recommended qualifying a second radio-chip supplier by the end of Q3 and keeping eight weeks of chip stock on hand.
No customer shipments were missed, because the warehouse held enough finished units to cover the gap.
